claims.text: The ability of noble metal–based high-entropy alloy nanoparticles to form a stable single-phase solid solution is primarily governed by kinetic limitations imposed by rapid heating and cooling.
Rapid heating and cooling can yield phase-separated nanoparticles.
Rapid heating and cooling can produce elemental segregation in these nanoparticles.
Rapid heating and cooling can produce uncontrolled nanoparticle morphologies.
An intermediate-temperature isothermal dwell enhances atomic diffusion.
Enhanced atomic diffusion during the dwell improves elemental mixing.
The dwell gives atoms sufficient time to overcome kinetic barriers associated with rapid temperature changes.
Additional diffusion time reduces phase separation.
Additional diffusion time reduces elemental segregation.
Reduced segregation and improved mixing promote formation of a uniform single-phase solid solution.
Adding an isothermal dwell will improve phase uniformity relative to rapid heating and cooling without a dwell.
Adding an isothermal dwell will reduce elemental segregation relative to the baseline.
Adding an isothermal dwell will produce more controlled and homogeneous particle morphology.
Adding an isothermal dwell will lower the effective thermal decomposition temperature.
The proposed mechanism applies to noble metal–based high-entropy alloy nanoparticles containing more than five elements under rapid thermal processing.
The intervention is relevant only when rapid processing limits diffusion enough to impede mixing.
The intervention consists of adding an intermediate-temperature isothermal dwell while holding composition and other processing conditions constant.
Failure of the dwell samples to exhibit statistically significant improvements, or observation of worsened thermal decomposition behavior, would falsify the hypothesis.
